cur:manuscripts-rossano-last-supper.summary: On the left Christ reclines at the end of a semicircular table with the apostles crowded around a single dish, one of them — Judas — reaching toward it; on the right Christ stoops to wash Peter's feet in a basin while the other disciples look on. Below, David and other prophets point upward. The two events of the night before the Passion are joined in one strip.
facts: The semicircular couch (sigma) and the reclining posture follow late Roman dining custom, as in other early images of the Last Supper.
The Wikipedia account of the manuscript notes the strange double perspective of this scene, in which the floor seems to tilt up into the table, decorated with birds.

cur:monumental2-tokali-nativity.summary: Against a brilliant blue ground the Virgin lies on a mattress beside the manger in which the swaddled Christ Child rests, while a host of angels bends over the scene from above; in the lower part two midwives prepare the Child's first bath. The deep ultramarine and the elegant, well-modelled figures are characteristic of the New Church's sophisticated workshop.
facts: The bathing of the newborn Christ by midwives, drawn from apocryphal tradition, became a standard part of Byzantine Nativity images, affirming the reality of the Incarnation.
The same composition appears in another Commons photograph labelled as Tokalı Kilise (TOKALIKILISE 057), which confirms the location of this unlabelled image.
cur:monumental2-tokali-nativity.notes: The Commons file has no location in its description and dates the painting to the 12th century; it is categorised under the Tokalı frescoes and matches a located photograph of the New Church Nativity, so the 10th-century date of the New Church is used here.

vam:O88818.summary: Carved from walrus ivory, this small cross-shaped relief shows Christ with arms rigidly outstretched and legs together on a footrest, his long hair falling to one shoulder and a cross-nimbus behind his head. Below the arms stand Longinus with the lance and Stephaton with the sponge, both unusually given haloes, while two angels fly towards the cross bearing wreaths and the Hand of God reaches down above Christ's head. The austere, linear figures carry a strong sense of the stillness of the cross.
facts: The V&A notes that showing only Longinus and Stephaton, without the Virgin and St John, is uncommon on ivories of the period, and that giving them haloes is a unique feature.
The eyes were once inlaid with jet beads, one of which survives in the left eye of Longinus.
Nineteen small holes suggest it was fixed to a book cover or reliquary; a larger hole at the top may mean it was later worn as a pectoral cross.
vam:O88818.notes: Anglo-Saxon, late 10th or early 11th century (V&A). Purchased at Sotheby's, London, 11 July 1923.
